title: When Scaffolding Breaks: Investigating Student Interaction with LLM-Based Writing Support in Real-Time K-12 EFL Classrooms
venue: Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
extended_summary:
This paper investigates how large language model (LLM)-based writing support functions in real-time K-12 English as a Foreign Language (EFL) classrooms, with particular attention to whether step-by-step AI scaffolding helps or hinders students under ordinary classroom constraints. The authors argue that most prior work examines asynchronous or higher-education contexts, leaving open questions about how LLM support operates in time-constrained, teacher-led middle school classrooms with students of varying proficiency levels.

To study this, the researchers developed WriteAid, a chat-based LLM writing support tool co-designed with a middle school English teacher. The tool offered several structured functions: sentence construction from Korean or code-mixed input, explanations of vocabulary and grammar, and grammar checking. Rather than giving direct answers, the system was prompted to provide scaffolded, step-by-step support. The team deployed WriteAid over six weeks during two writing assignments, collected 14,863 student-LLM messages from 133 consenting students, conducted qualitative coding of sampled interactions, observed three classroom sessions, and analyzed subsequent independent written assessments administered 2-3 weeks after the writing activities.

The study took place in a public middle school in South Korea with eighth-grade students aged 13-14 learning English at roughly beginner level. The classroom context was standard in-school EFL instruction, with 45-minute class periods and teacher supervision. Students used the system during regular classroom writing tasks, and their later essays were graded with an analytic rubric covering content, organization, vocabulary, and language use. The study also examined differences across high-, middle-, and low-performing students.

The main conclusions are that LLM-based support improved students' ability to produce grammatically correct sentences during classroom writing, but its scaffolded design had uneven effects across proficiency levels. Higher-performing students used the tool more efficiently and mainly delegated lower-order tasks such as vocabulary lookup or validation, whereas lower-performing students were more likely to outsource sentence generation and become confused or demotivated by step-by-step prompting. The classroom observations further suggest that LLM support changed teacher-student and peer dynamics: it reduced some teacher workload on simple questions, but also made it harder for teachers to identify struggling students and may have reduced peer interaction. Overall, the paper concludes that LLM writing support can be useful in middle school EFL classrooms, but only if designed with stronger attention to learner proficiency, classroom orchestration, and equity.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed deployment study with mixed quantitative and qualitative data, but it is not a controlled comparative design and does not estimate causal effects against a teacher-feedback or no-AI comparison. Evidence is informative and authentic but primarily observational with substantial threats to internal validity.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows promising immediate gains in grammatical correctness and teacher workflow efficiency, but effects are heterogeneous and partly adverse for lower-proficiency students, with no reported standardized effect sizes. Overall impact is therefore unclear/mixed rather than clearly positive.

interventions.use_case: Chat-based LLM scaffold (WriteAid) used in real-time middle school EFL writing classes to provide step-by-step support for sentence construction, grammar explanations, vocabulary help, and guided revision during in-class composition.
LLM-enabled writing support functioning as an EFL writing assistant for grammar correction, vocabulary translation, and sentence/paragraph revision within classroom writing tasks.

finding.finding_summary: In a six-week deployment with 133 consented eighth-grade students (157 total users), the LLM-supported writing tool improved students’ ability to produce grammatically correct sentences during in-class writing. During the fall semester, students constructed 632 sentences with AI assistance; 309 (48.9%) were incorporated verbatim into final essays, and 82.3% of those incorporated sentences were grammatically correct. However, transfer/retention into unsupported later writing varied sharply by proficiency: high-performing students correctly incorporated 65.8% of AI-constructed sentences into later written assessments, compared with 37.8% for middle-performing students and 14.0% for low-performing students, indicating stronger immediate surface-level support than durable independent writing gains for lower-proficiency learners.
finding.measure: Analytic writing assessment and grammar accuracy of AI-assisted sentences transferred into later unsupported essays; rubric domains included content, organization, vocabulary, and language use

finding.finding_summary: Qualitative analyses and classroom observations suggest the LLM scaffold had divergent motivational effects by proficiency. While some students engaged more as they became familiar with the system, lower- and middle-performing students showed much higher frequencies of confusion/annoyance during sessions (means of 11.4 and 12.2 negative affective responses per session, respectively) than high-performing students (3.8), and 69.2% of these negative responses occurred in the latter half of interaction, consistent with demotivation under time pressure and scaffold overload.
finding.measure: Observed and coded affective responses in student-LLM interactions, including confusion, annoyance, gratitude, and indifference; classroom observation notes
finding.study_size: Qualitative coding subset of 1,386 queries from 15 students; deployment n=133 consented students

finding.finding_summary: The study found that lower-proficiency students often outsourced higher-order writing tasks to the LLM, such as full or partial sentence generation, rather than applying grammar and composing independently. Authors interpret this as increased system reliance and weaker independent writing problem solving, whereas higher-performing students more often delegated lower-order tasks such as vocabulary translation and validation, preserving more learner agency over composition.
finding.measure: Qualitative coding of query types and interaction patterns, including full sentence generation, partial sentence generation, validation seeking, and revision behavior
finding.study_size: 1,386 coded queries from 15 sampled students; deployment n=133 consented students

finding.finding_summary: Classroom observations and teacher interview indicate the LLM improved efficiency by absorbing repetitive low-level questions about spelling, vocabulary, and basic grammar, allowing the teacher to spend more time circulating and checking progress. The teacher explicitly reported having more time to monitor students because they no longer needed to answer every simple question individually, although no quantitative workload reduction estimate was reported.
finding.measure: Naturalistic classroom observation and follow-up teacher interview about classroom workflow and teacher time allocation
finding.study_size: 3 observed class sessions; one teacher interview; deployment context n=157 students (133 consented for analysis)

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports classroom-level equity and orchestration challenges from introducing the LLM into real-time instruction. Although the tool appeared to narrow task-completion gaps by helping more lower-proficiency students finish assignments, it also made it harder for teachers to identify struggling students and shifted participation patterns so that extroverted students still dominated teacher attention while quieter students relied more heavily on the AI.
finding.measure: Naturalistic observation of classroom participation, teacher attention patterns, and follow-up teacher interview
finding.study_size: 3 observed class sessions; one teacher interview; deployment context n=157 students (133 consented for analysis)
